guide.summary: Rotation has its own versions of displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, and mass: angle, angular velocity, angular acceleration, torque, and rotational inertia. This unit covers rotational kinematics, torque, rotational inertia, Newton's second law for rotation, and static equilibrium.

sections.heading: Rotational kinematics
sections.body:
Angular quantities describe rotation about a fixed axis:

| Linear | Angular | Link (point at radius r) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| x (m) | θ (rad) | s = rθ |
| v (m/s) | ω (rad/s) | v = rω |
| a (m/s²) | α (rad/s²) | a_t = rα |

For constant α, the kinematic equations carry over directly:

ω = ω₀ + αt · θ = θ₀ + ω₀t + ½αt² · ω² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ

A wheel starting from rest with α = 2 rad/s² turns ½(2)(3²) = 9 rad in 3 s.

Every point on a rigid object has the same ω, but points farther from the axis move faster: v = rω.

sections.heading: Torque
sections.body:
Torque measures a force's ability to rotate an object about an axis:

τ = rF sin θ

where r is the distance from the axis to where the force acts, and θ is the angle between r and F. Equivalently, τ = r⊥F, using the **lever arm** (perpendicular distance from the axis to the force's line of action).

Pushing a door 0.8 m from the hinges with 10 N at 30° to the door gives τ = 0.8 × 10 × sin 30° = 4 N·m. Pushing perpendicular gives the maximum; pushing toward the hinge gives zero.

Assign signs: counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative (or vice versa, consistently).

sections.heading: Rotational inertia
sections.body:
Rotational inertia I is resistance to angular acceleration. It depends on mass **and how far the mass is from the axis**:

I = Σ m r² for point masses

For the same mass and radius, a hoop (all mass at the rim, I = MR²) has more rotational inertia than a solid disk (I = ½MR²). The exam gives formulas for specific shapes when needed.

Moving mass outward increases I sharply: doubling r for point masses quadruples I.

**Parallel axis theorem:** I = I_cm + Md², for an axis a distance d from a parallel axis through the center of mass. A uniform rod: I_cm = (1/12)ML², about one end (1/3)ML².

sections.heading: Newton's second law for rotation
sections.body:
τ_net = Iα

The same torque produces a smaller angular acceleration in an object with larger I. A disk and a hoop of equal mass and radius under equal torque: the disk spins up faster.

Combined problems link translation and rotation. A mass m hanging from a string wrapped around a pulley (radius R, inertia I):

mg − T = ma (hanging mass) · TR = Iα (pulley) · a = Rα (string doesn't slip)

Solving: a = mg/(m + I/R²). The pulley's inertia acts like extra mass, so a < g.

sections.heading: Static equilibrium
sections.body:
An object is in static equilibrium when

ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 (about **any** axis)

Choose the axis through an unknown force to eliminate it. For a uniform 4 m, 100 N beam on supports at both ends with a 200 N person 1 m from the left end, take torques about the left support:

R(4) = 100(2) + 200(1) = 400, so R = 100 N. Then ΣF = 0 gives L = 300 − 100 = 200 N.

The weight of a uniform object acts at its center. On a seesaw, balance means m₁r₁ = m₂r₂: a 30 kg child 2 m from the pivot balances a 40 kg child 1.5 m on the other side.

Zero net torque doesn't mean no rotation: it means constant angular velocity.

sections.heading: Exam tip
sections.body: For static equilibrium problems, choose the pivot at the location of an unknown force so its torque drops out, then write both ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0.

sections.heading: Connecting linear and rotational
sections.body: Each linear quantity has a rotational partner: displacement and angle, velocity and angular velocity, mass and rotational inertia, force and torque. Newton's second law becomes Στ = Iα.

keyTakeaways: ω, α, θ follow the same kinematic equations as v, a, x.
v = rω and a_t = rα link rotation to linear motion.
τ = rF sin θ; maximum when F is perpendicular to r.
I depends on mass distribution: mass farther from the axis means larger I.
Equilibrium: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0; pick the pivot at an unknown force.
commonMistakes: Using the full distance r when the force isn't perpendicular, without the sin θ.
Forgetting the weight of the beam itself in equilibrium problems.
Treating I as depending only on mass.
Mixing degrees and radians in ω and α calculations.
Assuming zero net torque means the object isn't rotating.
Forgetting the pulley's rotational inertia reduces the acceleration of a hanging mass.
examTips: State the axis you're calculating torques about.
In derivations, start from τ_net = Iα or Στ = 0 explicitly.
Free-body diagrams for rotation should show where each force acts, not just its direction.
Expect comparisons ("which reaches the bottom first") that hinge on I.
Check units: torque in N·m, I in kg·m², α in rad/s².
guide.cramSheet:
**Kinematics:** ω = ω₀ + αt · θ = ω₀t + ½αt² · ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ

**Links:** s = rθ · v = rω · a_t = rα

**Torque:** τ = rF sin θ = r⊥F

**Inertia:** I = Σmr² · hoop MR² · disk ½MR² · rod (center) ML²/12 · rod (end) ML²/3

**Parallel axis:** I = I_cm + Md²

**Newton II:** τ_net = Iα

**Equilibrium:** ΣF = 0, Στ = 0 · pivot at unknown force

**Pulley + mass:** a = mg/(m + I/R²)

vocab.definition: The angle, in radians, through which an object rotates.
Rate of change of angular displacement, ω, in rad/s.
Rate of change of angular velocity, α, in rad/s².
The rotational effect of a force about an axis: τ = rF sin θ.
The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of a force.
An object's resistance to angular acceleration; depends on mass and its distribution relative to the axis.
I = I_cm + Md² for an axis parallel to one through the center of mass, at distance d.
Net torque equals rotational inertia times angular acceleration: τ_net = Iα.
A state in which net force and net torque on an object are both zero and it is at rest.
Net torque is zero, so angular velocity is constant.
Linear speed of a point on a rotating object, v = rω.
The point where an object's weight can be considered to act for torque calculations.
The angle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius; 2π rad = 360°.

practice.stem: A 20 N force is applied perpendicular to a wrench, 0.5 m from the bolt. What torque does it produce about the bolt?
A wheel turns one full revolution every 2 s at a steady rate. What is its angular velocity?
practice.explanation: One revolution is 2π rad. ω = 2π/2 = π rad/s.

distractors.B: Forgot to divide by the 2 s period.
distractors.C: Gave revolutions per second instead of radians per second.

practice.stem: A hoop and a solid disk have the same mass and radius. Which has greater rotational inertia about its center?

choices.text: They are equal, because they have the same mass and radius
The disk, because it has more material near the center
The hoop, because all its mass is at the maximum distance from the axis
It depends on how fast they rotate

practice.explanation: I = Σmr². The hoop's mass is all at r = R; the disk's is spread from 0 to R. Hoop: MR²; disk: ½MR².

distractors.D: I is a property of shape and axis.
distractors.A: Rotational inertia depends on mass distribution, not just mass.

practice.stem: Which conditions must hold for an object to be in static equilibrium?

choices.text: All forces on the object are equal in magnitude.
Net force is zero and net torque is zero.

practice.explanation: Zero net force prevents translational acceleration; zero net torque prevents angular acceleration.

distractors.B: Two equal, opposite, offset forces give zero net force but nonzero torque.

practice.stem: A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where should a 40 kg child sit on the other side to balance it? (Ignore the seesaw's mass.)

practice.topic: 5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form
practice.stem: A net torque of 6 N·m acts on a wheel with rotational inertia 2 kg·m². What is its angular acceleration?
A wheel starts from rest and has constant angular acceleration 2 rad/s². Through what angle does it turn in the first 3 s?

distractors.B: That's the final angular velocity in rad/s.

practice.stem: A person pushes on a door 0.8 m from its hinges with a 10 N force directed at 30° to the plane of the door. What torque does the force produce about the hinges?
practice.explanation: The angle between r (along the door) and F is 30°. τ = 0.8 × 10 × sin 30° = 4 N·m.

practice.stem: A point on a spinning wheel is 0.3 m from the axle. The wheel spins at 10 rad/s. What is the point's linear speed?

distractors.D: Assumed every point moves at ω.

practice.stem: A uniform 4.0 m beam weighing 100 N rests horizontally on supports at each end. A 200 N person stands 1.0 m from the left end. What upward force does the right support exert?
practice.explanation: Torques about the left support: R(4.0) = 100(2.0) + 200(1.0) = 400 N·m, so R = 100 N. (The left support then provides 300 − 100 = 200 N.)

distractors.D: Left out the beam's own weight.
distractors.A: Split the 300 N total weight evenly, ignoring where the person stands.

practice.topic: 5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form
practice.stem: A block of mass m hangs from a light string wrapped around a pulley of radius R and rotational inertia I. The pulley turns on a frictionless axle and the string doesn't slip. What is the magnitude of the block's acceleration?
practice.explanation: Block: mg − T = ma. Pulley: TR = Iα = Ia/R, so T = Ia/R². Then mg = a(m + I/R²).

distractors.B: Ignores the pulley's resistance to rotation.
distractors.A: Wrote T = IaR² by mistake; units don't work.

practice.topic: 5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form
practice.stem: Equal torques are applied to a solid disk and a hoop of the same mass and radius, both starting from rest. After the same time, which has the greater angular velocity?

choices.text: The disk, because its smaller rotational inertia gives a larger angular acceleration
The hoop, because its mass is farther from the axis
They are equal, because the torques and masses are equal
The hoop, because it has larger rotational inertia

practice.explanation: α = τ/I. I_disk = ½MR² < I_hoop = MR², so α_disk = 2α_hoop and ω = αt is twice as large.

distractors.D: Larger I means smaller α for the same torque.

practice.stem: Two small, equal masses are fixed on a light rod at distance r on either side of the rotation axis. A constant torque gives the system angular acceleration α. If both masses are moved to distance 2r, what is the new angular acceleration under the same torque?
practice.explanation: I = 2mr² becomes 2m(2r)² = 4(2mr²). α = τ/I falls to one quarter.

distractors.B: Treated I as proportional to r instead of r².

practice.stem: The net torque on a spinning object about its center of mass is zero. Which must be true?

choices.text: The net force on it is zero.

practice.explanation: τ_net = Iα = 0 means α = 0, so ω stays constant (possibly nonzero).

distractors.B: Zero torque doesn't stop existing rotation.
distractors.A: Forces through the center of mass can produce zero torque but nonzero net force.

practice.prompt: A uniform rod of mass M and length L is attached to a wall by a frictionless hinge at its left end. A vertical string attached to the right end holds the rod horizontal and at rest. The rotational inertia of the rod about the hinge is (1/3)ML².

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe a free-body diagram for the rod, showing each force and where it acts.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the tension in the string in terms of M and g.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude and direction of the force the hinge exerts on the rod.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The string is cut. Derive an expression for the rod's angular acceleration immediately after the string is cut, in terms of g and L.

rubric.description: Weight Mg downward, tension T upward, hinge force (vertical) — and no others.
Weight at the center (L/2), tension at the right end, hinge force at the left end.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Three forces act on the rod: its weight Mg downward at the center (L/2 from the hinge); the string's tension T upward at the right end (L from the hinge); and the hinge force F_h at the left end. Because the other two forces are vertical, F_h is vertical too.

(b) Taking torques about the hinge, F_h has no lever arm. Στ = 0: T·L − Mg(L/2) = 0, so T = Mg/2.

(c) ΣF_y = 0: F_h + T − Mg = 0, so F_h = Mg − Mg/2 = Mg/2, directed upward.

(d) Immediately after the cut, only the weight produces torque about the hinge. τ = Iα: Mg(L/2) = (1/3)ML²α, so α = (MgL/2)/(ML²/3) = 3g/(2L).
